newsitem.title: ITALY: Mafia rackets bleeding Italian businesses - study.
newsitem.headline: Mafia rackets bleeding Italian businesses - study.

text.p: Italy's small businesses are forced to pay the Mafia some $12 billion a year in extortion and loansharking rackets -- almost the amount the government wants to cut from its budget deficit, a retailer's group said on Tuesday.
In its latest study, the Confesercenti organisation, which represents shopkeepers and retailers, said a parallel "tax" imposed by the Mob was bleeding the country's small businessmen.
"The study points to a 'parallel state' that uses it own collection system..." the group's report said.

"Organised crime is a real regime that imposes its taxes, offers its services -- such as protection and loans -- and dictates its rules without any qualms about punishing those who do not want to respect them," the study said.
The study said Italy's shopkeepers and small businesses pay out 15 trillion lire to loansharks and some 7.2 trillion lire in extortion rackets.
This total of 22.2 trillion lire ($12 billion) is just short of the 25 trillion lire the government wants to trim from its 1998 budget deficit.

"A large part of these resources could be recovered by the legal economy and produce new development and jobs and in turn provide new revenue for the state," said Confesercenti secretary-general Marco Venturi.
Small businesses and shops lose another $3 billion to petty crime and fraud each year, the study showed.
The study was based on reports from businesses and some 8,000 calls to the hotline "SOS Business", which the association has set up to help stem organised crime's control.
It showed that small businesses falling victim to Mafia loansharks were often forced to close within three years because they could not keep up with exorbitant interests rates imposed by mobsters.
The Mafia and its organised crime affiliates throughout the country employ an army of some 25,000 loan collectors, known as "strozzini," literally "stranglers", the study said.
Police estimate there are as many as 40,000 "strozzini" in the southern Campania region alone. Campania is home to the Naples-based Camorra, the local version of the Mafia.

Italian loansharks in the Naples area have been known to demand interest rates of up to 30 percent a month, according to Father Massimo Rastrelli, a Jesuit priest who set up an anti-usury solidarity fund to help Neapolitans.
Organised crime groups, particularly in the south, have often used violence to force businessmen to pay in protection and extortion rackets.
Businessmen rarely stand up to the racketeers. One who did, Palermo factory owner Libero Grassi, paid with his life.
He was shot in 1991 and mourned as a national hero for his courageous stand. Grassi's public refusal to pay up led to the arrest of several members of a Mafia extortion gang in the Sicilian capital.
The study said that since the start of the decade, some 250,000 shops and small businesses had been forced to close.

While most had to shut down because of economic pressures and competition from large retail chains, a growing number were forced to close because of the pressures from organised crime. ($1=1,792 lire)
